question.problem:
Consider the polar curve $r={cos}^{3}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{3}⁡(\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )={cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )({cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\theta )),
$$

and ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results.*

$$
\begin{aligned}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\to {0}^{-}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{-} \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\to {0}^{+}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{+}\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & ={cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})({cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =0(0-3) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{+},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )({cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\theta ))}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{3}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{\cancel{{cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )}({cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\theta ))}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{\cancel{3}}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\theta )}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the limit in the numerator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}({cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\theta )) & ={cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0-3\cdot 1 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the second hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\theta )}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{-3}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, and the first hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\theta )}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{-3}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14272061/assets/8e0aded769ce741411085da3c68bc26b92c5568dd19e8e60f416615e5f849558.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."
